questions.prompt: The matrix norm induced by a vector norm is
questions.explanation: The induced norm is the operator norm: the greatest stretch of a unit vector, which is also \(\sup_{x \ne 0} \lVert Ax \rVert / \lVert x \rVert\). Adding every absolute entry is not that maximum, and neither is a product of singular values. A diagonal entry is one stretch only when the matching basis vector is a maximizer.

the sum of the absolute values of the entries
the product of the singular values

questions.explanation: Absolute column sums are \(\lvert 1 \rvert + \lvert 2 \rvert = 3\) and \(\lvert -4 \rvert + \lvert 3 \rvert = 7\). The induced 1-norm is the larger one, 7. The row sums are both 5, so 5 is the infinity-norm. The trace 4 and the largest entry 4 are not column sums.

questions.prompt: The infinity-norm induced by the vector infinity-norm equals
questions.explanation: Rows are what the infinity-norm inspects: add absolute entries across each row and keep the largest sum. Column sums define the induced 1-norm. The largest singular value is the induced 2-norm. The Frobenius norm uses squares of entries instead of a single row.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>2 by 2 matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   -4</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   3</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with first row 1, -4 and second row 2, 3.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order you would use to compute an induced 1-norm.
questions.explanation: The induced 1-norm is a maximum of column sums of absolute values, so the absolute values come first, the sums second, and the maximum third. Reporting a row sum instead computes the infinity-norm. Taking the maximum entry before summing misses every column that has two nonzero numbers. The matrix in the figure is only a picture of a 2 by 2 array; the steps do not depend on its particular entries.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>2 by 2 matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   -4</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   3</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with first row 1, -4 and second row 2, 3.
steps: Replace every entry by its absolute value.
Add the absolute values down each column.
Keep the largest of those column sums.
Report that largest sum as the induced 1-norm.

questions.prompt: What is the induced infinity-norm of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -4 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)?
questions.explanation: Absolute row sums are \(\lvert 1 \rvert + \lvert -4 \rvert = 5\) and \(\lvert 2 \rvert + \lvert 3 \rvert = 5\). The induced infinity-norm is 5. The larger column sum is 7, which is the 1-norm of this same matrix. The largest entry is 4, and that entry is not a row sum.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>2 by 2 matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   -4</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   3</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with first row 1, -4 and second row 2, 3.

questions.explanation: The singular values of a diagonal matrix are the absolute values of the diagonal entries, here 3 and 5. The induced 2-norm is the larger singular value, 5. The signed entry \(-5\) is not a norm. The sum \(3+5 = 8\) is the nuclear norm, and the square root of \(9+25\) is the Frobenius norm.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>diagonal matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">3   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   -5</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A diagonal 2 by 2 matrix with diagonal entries 3 and -5.

questions.prompt: Let \(a > 0\). Write the induced 1-norm of \(\begin{bmatrix} a & -a \\ 2a & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) as an expression in the name a.
questions.explanation:
With \(a > 0\), the absolute column sums are \(\lvert a \rvert + \lvert 2a \rvert = 3a\) and \(\lvert -a \rvert + 0 = a\). The induced 1-norm is the larger sum, \(3a\).
• \(2a\) is the common absolute row sum, so it is the infinity-norm of this matrix.
• \(4a\) adds every absolute entry and does not discard the smaller column.
• \(a\) keeps the smaller column and misses the column that holds both \(a\) and \(2a\).

questions.explanation: \(A^T A = \mathrm{diag}(0, 36)\), so the singular values are 0 and 6. The induced 2-norm is 6. The only nonzero entry already has absolute value 6, which happens to match, but the matching reason is the singular value, not the rule that a norm equals its largest entry. A column sum gives the same 6 here and is the 1-norm, a different definition.

questions.prompt: For an induced matrix norm, which relation holds for every vector \(x\)?
questions.explanation: The induced norm is defined as the maximum of \(\lVert Ax \rVert / \lVert x \rVert\), so the inequality points that way: the stretch of one particular \(x\) cannot exceed the maximum. The reverse inequality would say every vector attains the maximum. Adding the two norms is not a product bound. A sum on the right is a different estimate and is not the operator-norm inequality.

questions.prompt: One of these steps is false. Select that step, and the reason it fails. The matrix is \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
questions.explanation: The largest entry really is 1, and the last step only applies the rule stated just above it. The false step is the rule. The induced 2-norm is the largest singular value. Here \(A\) is symmetric with eigenvalues 2 and 0, because \(A(1,1) = (2,2)\), so the 2-norm is 2 rather than 1. A column-sum formula would compute the 1-norm, which is also 2 for this matrix, and it is not what the flawed step claimed. Singular values are nonnegative, so a sign correction is not the issue.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>matrix of ones</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   1</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with every entry equal to 1.
steps: Let \(A\) be the \(2 \times 2\) matrix whose four entries are all 1.
The largest absolute entry of \(A\) is 1.
The induced 2-norm of a matrix equals its largest absolute entry.
Applying that rule to \(A\) produces the value 1.
reasons: The induced 2-norm is the largest singular value, which is 2 for this matrix, not the largest entry.
Column sums define the infinity-norm, so the step should have added across a row.
Singular values of a symmetric matrix are allowed to be negative, and that is the missing sign.

questions.prompt: For symmetric \(A\), the gradient of \(\tfrac12 x^T A x\) is \(Ax\), and its Lipschitz constant is the induced 2-norm of \(A\). What is that constant when \(A = \mathrm{diag}(4, 7)\)?
questions.explanation: The singular values are the absolute eigenvalues 4 and 7, so the induced 2-norm is 7. That is the Lipschitz constant. The other eigenvalue 4 is a stretch in a different direction, not the worst one. The trace 11 adds the eigenvalues, and the determinant 28 multiplies them.

questions.prompt: When \(A\) is real and symmetric, the induced 2-norm equals
questions.explanation: A real symmetric matrix has singular values equal to the absolute values of its eigenvalues, and the induced 2-norm keeps the largest of those. A negative eigenvalue still contributes its absolute value: \(\mathrm{diag}(1,-6)\) has 2-norm 6, not \(-6\) and not 1. The trace adds every eigenvalue, and the largest entry need not be an eigenvalue at all. This extreme stretch is the curvature bound a descent argument spends.
